text: Every PNG file begins with the same 8 bytes (hex 89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A). The PNG specification says this signature 'differentiates a PNG datastream from other types of datastream and allows early detection of some transmission errors.'
why: Gives the exact signature the teacher paraphrased and why it exists.

text: A binary header must also fix the byte order of its integers. PNG stores all multi-byte integers in network byte order (most significant byte first), while Parquet stores its 4-byte metadata length little-endian; a decoder that assumes the wrong order reads garbage sizes.
why: The 4-byte version and index-size fields only work if encoder and decoder agree on endianness.

text: A Parquet file is laid out as 'PAR1', the column chunks, the file metadata, a 4-byte metadata length, and 'PAR1' again. Metadata is written after the data 'to allow for single pass writing', and readers first read it to find the column chunks they need.
why: Shows the footer alternative to the lecture's header design and why a writer might prefer it.

text: Putting the directory at the end is a common alternative to a header: a ZIP archive ends with its central directory and end-of-central-directory record, and MP4 muxers usually write the moov index at the end, with a 'faststart' pass that moves it to the beginning.
why: Header vs footer is a real design choice; the lecture only shows the header side.

text: RFC 4180 lets a CSV file have an optional first line of column names, and the text/csv MIME type has a 'header' parameter (present or absent) saying whether it is there. That header names columns; it does not say where data lies.
why: Avoids confusion when readers meet 'CSV header' elsewhere.

text: As of October 2026, MDN lists Safari as the only browser that displays TIFF natively; other browsers need special libraries or add-ons, so TIFF is still avoided for web images.
why: Shows the teacher's example still holds and names the browser that does have a decoder.

text: NIST defines 1 MB as 10^6 bytes and 1 MiB as 2^20 = 1,048,576 bytes; for memory, 'megabyte' is often used for the binary size, so the two readings differ by about 5%.
why: Clarifies the 'M stands for a million' point.

text: The student's numbers come from real databases: PostgreSQL stores every table and index as fixed-size pages, usually 8 kB (PostgreSQL 18). Page-based B+ trees matter when an index is too big for RAM, which is not the case for this dictionary.
why: Explains why the proposal was reasonable in general yet over-engineered here.

text: AWS's Well-Architected Framework makes cost optimization one of its six pillars: a cost-optimized workload 'achieves an outcome at the lowest possible price point, and meets your functional requirements.'
why: A primary source for the teacher's cost-first principle.
